segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Let's look again at how we speak about the future in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We saw that we have a future tense, but we might not use it very often because, firstly, we can just use the present to talk about the future if we have some future context, some word like mañana, tomorrow, later, más tarde, or even another part of the sentence which shows us that we're talking about the future, we can just use the present.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: When we don't have that, we can use ir a, to go to, so voy a, vamos a, vas a, which is also present tense — voy, vas, vamos, it's present — but we can use it to talk about the future.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, for example, bailar, bailar, b-a-i-l-a-r, means to dance.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We can relate it to ballerina, ballerina actually is just dancer in Spanish, bailarín in Spanish is dancer, so that's where we get ballerina from, bailar. So if you want to say we are going to dance...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you had some future context, like later, más tarde, or literally more late, you could just say we dance later.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Bailamos más tarde. But you could have used that structure with vamos if you wanted to, you have the option. We can say bailamos más tarde or we could say we're going to dance later.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Vamos a bailar más tarde. So we saw that we have a future tense. We have a future tense, although we might not need to use it very often because we have this situation in Spanish that we can use the present or that ir a, to go to, is used even more often than in English, this structure of I'm going to do it instead of I'll do it is used even more in Spanish than in English. But we do have a future tense, and the future tense is luckily very related to the different versions that we found of the verb haber. Haber was a very irregular verb, this to have that we use to go into the past. What was the trick that we used to find the different versions of this very irregular verb haber?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: We use the vowels, the e and a sounds.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. We used these to take off from. We go, what are the two vowels in haber? E and a. Okay, e by itself means...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I have. And a by itself means...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He, she, it, or you formal have.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Perfect. And from these we can find the other versions. So we have he for I have, and we have is...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hemos. And we have ha for he, she, it, you formal. For you informal, what would we do to ha?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Has. H-a-s, now completely silent this h, this h that we find in all of these forms. They have or you guys have?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Han. So these are our different versions of haber. Now, these very sounds, so the sounds because we're not including the h, the sounds e, emos, a, as, an, are the same sounds that we add onto the to-form of the verb to get this future tense. So we have a verb like bailar, to dance. If I want to say I will dance using this future tense, I can look at how is I have from haber, so how is I have from haber?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: He. And I can just stick it on the end. But it's the sound that is the same, what we are sticking on the end of the verb is an e, not a h-e. So, I will dance?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The ending takes the accent. And we said that in Spanish we are pushing the accent into the future, which is an interesting phenomenon. We spoke about how in Greek, for example, in the past you pull it back into the past. So we find this phenomenon occurring in other languages as well. Here we are literally pushing the accent into the future and we accent that ending, and we say bailaré. Bailaré, I will dance. We will dance?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Bailaremos. He, she, it, you formal will dance?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Bailará. They or you guys will dance?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Bailarás. Good. So we get the future tense without having to learn anything new, huh? We just have to remember that we can look back at haber and see what the different versions of haber were, and then use them to build our future. So in fact, we have two future tenses, let's say. We have will and would. They're both future tenses. Now, -é, -emos, -á, -ás, -án, they work for all verbs: -er, -ir, -ar, it doesn't matter, they are all using these sounds to form will.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And we have the same situation with would. -er, -ir, -ar verbs, they are all together. And our key sound for would is -ía. So we add on -ía to the end of the verb. We are accenting it again, because it's pushing the accent into the future, and this -ía actually gives us I, he, she, it, and you formal. So here I is jumping in with he, she, it, and you formal. So bailaría, bailaría means I would dance, he would dance, she would dance, you formal would dance, or it would dance if you can think of some context where that would make sense.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I think you can work out what the rest would be. So let's try. How would you say we would dance?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. The only thing is the accent stays on the ía.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Bailaríamos. Good. They or you guys?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So that's it, that's would.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So the would and will share some characteristics as they are both different futures, no? They share the characteristic that we are adding onto the full verb: bailar, bailaré, I will dance; bailar, bailaría, I would dance. And they share the characteristic that they are stressing the ending, that the accent is going to the ending. And they share the characteristic that for both futures we group all the verbs together: -ar, -er, -ir verbs. So for both futures we have one set of endings for all verb types.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, iría. So this actually works for I, he, she, it, and you formal. So in the would tense we have I jumping in with he, she, it, you formal. How would you say she wouldn't go?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No iría. Good. What was to eat?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comer. How would you say I would eat?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. I would eat, but I don't have time.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tempo, tempo we have in English.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comería, pero no tengo tiempo. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Transformar. How would you say it would transform?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Transformaría. This you would use it if it was to say it would transform something else, no? So you could say it would transform the situation. How would you say that? It would transform the situation.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Transformaría la situación. If you wanted to say it would transform and you mean it would get transformed, it would undergo a transformation, then in Spanish you will say it would transform itself. Now in English, we just use the context to understand whether we mean to transform something else or it would transform, it would get transformed. But in Spanish, most of the time you're going to want to put that itself. What is that itself?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Itself, se. It would get transformed?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Contaminar. Good. If you want to say it contaminates, how would you say it, it contaminates, present tense?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Contamina. So contamina would mean it contaminates, it's contaminating, no? Maybe we're talking about a factory and we say contamina.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If we want to say it gets contaminated, we don't really have this gets in Spanish, no? So in Spanish to give this meaning of it gets contaminated, we would just say it contaminates itself. Now it doesn't mean that it's responsible for its own contamination, or that it is literally contaminating itself. It's just a structure that we use to replace this gets that we don't have in Spanish. So if we want to say it gets contaminated and we're talking about a river, we would just say it contaminates itself, even though we all understand that what we don't mean is that the river is actually contaminating itself. So how would you say that, it contaminates itself or it gets contaminated?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say it would get contaminated? So it's not it would contaminate, it's it would get contaminated.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Imaginar. Well done for converting the j to j. Imagination, imaginación, imaginar. I imagine?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Imagino. You will often hear in Spanish, I imagine myself. How would that be?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me imagino. And here it doesn't really change the meaning. Sometimes adding this myself or herself, itself, yourself, etc., doesn't really change the meaning very much. Imagino, me imagino, I imagine. How would you say I would imagine?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I would imagine that he doesn't want to go. What is this that that we use? It's the same as what.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So all together, I would imagine that he doesn't want to go.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me imaginaría que no quiere ir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Me imaginaría que no quiere ir.
